title: Racism is international; Europe favouring bigger-name Americans
summary: Waters says racism exists in Paris too and that European promoters often preferred big-name Black Americans like Sonny Stitt to him; he recalls leading an integrated California band in the 1940s.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Well, those two things I just cited, the avoiding racism and getting more respect as
Benny Waters JOHP 6/6/82
an artist - are those important factors in the fact that you spent 30 years in Europe?

Ah, that racism I've seen, I think that's international, you know? They have racism here in Paris, too, you'll see, particularly now, you know? And as far as the other thing is concerned, you have to come home back from Europe, but it's, you run through a little form of jealousy. [ ] this is sometimes the musicians that play well. They don't want to work with an ordinary musician that plays as well. They won't work with [a] negro - if they work with a negro they prefer to work with [a] big name negro that can lift them up, understand what I mean? That exists, 'cause that exists with me.
Right. And for a while you weren't a big enough name -
That's right -
but now finally you are, so now you're gettin' in on - but even so it still exists for you -
That is, now it don't matter, see. 'Cause I make enough money because -
Right -
if I don't make it here I go to another country, I mean [ ], like I was saying, it's -

So it wasn't the same kind of racism as you would have encountered here in the States, but you felt yourself a victim of European bands, European concert halls in general, the jazz scene in Europe signifying using bigger name black Americans than they were with you.
That's right. Which that makes sense in a way, I figured too, commercially, maybe -
Right -
Because I - everybody knows Benny Waters, so they'd rather have the Sonny Stitts.
Right. So it wasn't just racism, it was also the fact that you were, since you lived there they'd rather bring someone over sometimes.
It was two things, 'cause I've seen it, two things because I've heard guys, the older ones, I heard [ ] -

Right. But you do feel that to - and you say even more today that there's an internationalism to the racism, that you could have a problem being a black in France just as much as here in the United States of America.
Benny Waters JOHP 6/6/82 106

Yeah, international, that's international. That's international. I mean, 'cause first they got me in the irons [?] , a band in California, I have a band in California. And I had a Mexican, I had an Indian and a white boy. I had a white boy that used to work with Jan Garber, playing saxophone with him.
Uh huh.
That was years ago.
And that was in the '40's, yeah.
Yeah. See what I'm talking about?
